subsection: 8. Case study: the Jarrow March, October 1936

notes.h: The national setting: the Depression and the government
notes.b: Jarrow's story only makes sense against the national picture. After the world slump of 1929, Britain had mass unemployment that fell unevenly, and the government believed time would cure it.
points: Registered unemployment in Britain peaked at nearly three million in 1932-33 and was under two million in 1936. The Depression (the world slump in trade and production after 1929) hit hardest in the old staple industries such as shipbuilding.

Recovery was uneven: the north of England, South Wales and central Scotland, where the staple industries were concentrated, stayed depressed, while the south-east and Midlands recovered. This is why Jarrow could be in crisis while the nation's figures improved.

Stanley Baldwin, the Conservative leader, was Prime Minister of the National Government from 1935. His government kept to orthodox finance and balanced budgets, believing general recovery would in time reach the depressed areas, so it saw no need for special action.

The long-term unemployed were paid by the Unemployment Assistance Board, set up under the Unemployment Act 1934. It paid benefit, the dole, only after a household means test, which examined the whole family's income.
The Special Areas Act 1934 designated depressed areas, including Durham and Tyneside, where Jarrow lay. Commissioners were appointed, but with limited funds, so the town got little help.
Before the march the government's attitude was summed up by Walter Runciman, President of the Board of Trade, who told Jarrow it must "work out its own salvation".
notes.tip: Keep Baldwin and Runciman apart. Runciman, at the Board of Trade, said Jarrow must work out its own salvation; Baldwin, the Prime Minister, was the one who refused to meet the marchers. Give no year for Runciman's remark.

notes.b: Jarrow was a one-industry town, so its fortunes rose and fell with a single shipyard. When the yard failed, almost everything else in the town failed with it.
points: Jarrow lies on the south bank of the River Tyne in County Durham and had a population of about 35,000.

Charles Mark Palmer founded the shipyard in 1851. The firm later became Palmers Shipbuilding and Iron Company, with its own blast furnaces and steelworks, so it grew into a combined shipyard and iron and steel works that dominated the town.
Almost the whole local economy depended on the yard's wages, so when orders collapsed, the shops, trades and families that lived off those wages collapsed with it.
Palmers' last ship, the destroyer HMS Duchess, was launched in 1932, and a receiver (an official appointed to take over a failed company's affairs) was appointed in 1933.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Charles Mark Palmer, founder of the yard in 1851, with Sir John Jarvis, who helped later, or David Riley, who led the march.

notes.h: Why the yard closed: slump, NSS and the steelworks refusal
notes.b: Palmers did not simply fail by accident. A world slump in shipbuilding, then a deliberate scheme by the industry itself, closed the yard, and a second body then blocked the one plan to replace it.
points: World trade fell and foreign competition grew, so British yards had far more capacity than orders. This is the thinking behind the scheme that closed Palmers.

National Shipbuilders Security Ltd (NSS) was formed in 1930 by the shipbuilding firms, with Bank of England support. It bought and closed redundant yards, financed by a levy (a compulsory charge) on shipbuilders.
NSS bought Palmers in 1934 and dismantled the yard. The site could not be used for shipbuilding for forty years, which ruled out any revival of shipbuilding in Jarrow.
In 1934 T. Vosper Salt proposed a modern steelworks on the Palmers site. The British Iron and Steel Federation opposed it, because it wanted no new competitor, and the scheme was dropped.
Wilkinson's later book blamed NSS, the steel interests and the government for what happened to the town.
notes.tip: Examiners want causes that go beyond the word unemployment. Name the single-industry town, NSS closing the yard in 1934, the steelworks refusal and government inaction, and keep NSS (closed the yard) separate from the British Iron and Steel Federation (blocked the steelworks).

notes.h: Unemployment and social conditions in Jarrow
notes.b: The closure left Jarrow with unemployment far above the national level and the poverty that goes with it.
points: In the mid-1930s about two-thirds to over 70 per cent of Jarrow's insured workers were unemployed. Figures quoted vary, so give the range, not one exact figure.
National insured unemployment in 1936 was about 13 per cent, so Jarrow's rate was several times the national one.
Jarrow had one of the worst records in Britain for poor and overcrowded housing, poverty, hunger, ill health and high death rates.
J.B. Priestley visited Jarrow for his book English Journey (1934) and described it as a town without work or hope, which makes his book a useful source on conditions.
Wilkinson later called her book on Jarrow The Town That Was Murdered, because she held that the town had been killed by decisions made elsewhere.
notes.tip: Never give a single exact unemployment figure for Jarrow. Use the range, and compare it with the national figure of about 13 per cent in 1936.

notes.h: Key figure: Ellen Wilkinson and the organisers
notes.b: The march was run by the town council with cross-party support, and its public face was the town's Labour MP, Ellen Wilkinson.
points: Ellen Wilkinson (1891-1947), known as Red Ellen for her politics and red hair, was an early member of the Communist Party of Great Britain, which she left in the 1920s. She was a trade union organiser and Labour MP for Middlesbrough East from 1924 to 1931.
She was elected Labour MP for Jarrow in 1935, so she spoke for a constituency whose plight she had known for only a short time before the march.
She backed the march and did much of the publicity, speeches and parliamentary work, including presenting the petition in the Commons. She was a participant, but not on foot for the whole way.

She left the march early on to attend the Labour Party conference in Edinburgh and rejoined it later. She did not share the men's sleeping quarters, so her account is that of an organiser, not an ordinary marcher.
Councillor David Riley was the marshal and leader of the marchers on the road, so Wilkinson led the campaign and Riley led the column.
Jarrow Borough Council organised the march, and Labour, Conservatives and Liberals on the council supported it, so it was presented as an appeal by the whole town, not a party or Communist protest.

Wilkinson wrote The Town That Was Murdered in 1939, partly blaming NSS, the steel interests and the government. After the war she became Minister of Education in the Labour government of 1945 and died in 1947.
Historians treat her book as the account of a partisan participant, written in 1939 with hindsight, which gives it great value as a source but means it needs care.
notes.tip: On Wilkinson's role, say organiser and publicist who joined the march but did not walk all of it or sleep with the men. Do not say she walked the whole way.

notes.h: The Crusade: aims, organisation and preparations
notes.b: The organisers called the march a crusade, not a hunger march, and prepared it carefully so that it would look respectable and non-political.
points: The aim was a petition asking the government to provide work for Jarrow, above all by bringing new industry such as a steelworks, and to make the town's distress known.
About 200 men were chosen from many more volunteers and each was medically examined, so that only fit men set out.
The men carried a petition of about 11,000 signatures in an oak box. Their banner read Jarrow Crusade, and a mouth-organ band kept up their spirits and set the pace.
They were organised and disciplined to show that the unemployed were respectable men who wanted work. A public appeal raised funds, and supporters gave boots, clothing and food.

The national Labour Party and the TUC (the Trades Union Congress, the federation of trade unions) gave no official support, because they feared Communist links and preferred action through Parliament.
The Labour conference in Edinburgh in October 1936 criticised the march, although many local Labour parties and trades councils helped it.

The Communist-led National Unemployed Workers' Movement (NUWM) had a tradition of hunger marches that the government and the Labour leadership distrusted. Jarrow kept apart from it, which is why the town called its march a crusade.

The churches gave a service and the Bishop of Jarrow's blessing at the start, and churches along the route gave food and shelter. Herbert Hensley Henson, Bishop of Durham, condemned the march as revolutionary mob pressure.
notes.tip: Do not call the Jarrow march a hunger march or a Communist march. It was cross-party and deliberately kept apart from the NUWM. Also, Labour's national leadership withheld official support, but it did not oppose the cause and local Labour parties helped.

notes.b: The men walked from the north-east to London, relying on the hospitality of the towns along the way, and the sympathetic press turned their walk into a national story.
points: The marchers left Jarrow on 5 October 1936 after a church service and a send-off by crowds.

They walked about 300 miles by way of Chester-le-Street, Darlington, Ripon, Harrogate, Leeds, Barnsley, Sheffield, Chesterfield, Nottingham, Leicester, Market Harborough, Northampton, Bedford, Luton and St Albans.
They marched in stages with rests and Sundays off, and slept in drill halls, schools, church halls and sometimes workhouses, relying on supporters for meals.

They were welcomed and fed by councils, Co-operative societies, churches and local parties of all sides. At Leicester, Co-operative boot workers repaired the marchers' boots, although some officials and Conservatives were cool.
The march was widely covered by the press and by newsreels (short films shown in cinemas), mostly sympathetically, which made it a national story.
They reached London (Marble Arch) on 31 October 1936, and a meeting was held in Hyde Park on 1 November 1936.
notes.tip: Learn the dates: left Jarrow 5 October 1936, reached London 31 October. For route or routine questions, name some towns, the banner and the band, and say where they slept.

notes.h: The government's response and the petition
notes.b: The government met the march with a refusal to act. The petition was presented, but it brought no new commitment.
points: In October 1936 the government stated that marches on London were undesirable and that grievances should be raised through MPs, because processions had no constitutional influence.
Stanley Baldwin, the Prime Minister, refused to receive a deputation of the marchers.
Ellen Wilkinson presented the petition in the House of Commons on 4 November 1936. It led only to a brief exchange and no action.
The Unemployment Assistance Board reduced the marchers' benefit, the dole cut, because they had not been available for work while they were marching.
The marchers returned to Jarrow by train on 5 November 1936. They were welcomed home, but there was bitter disappointment among the men.
The government's argument was that national recovery would restore jobs in time, and it questioned whether special help for one town was fair when many areas suffered.
notes.tip: Keep three dates apart: arrival in London on 31 October, the petition on 4 November and the return home on 5 November. For the government's case, cite who issued the statement, and set its argument about MPs and constitutional influence against the town's distress.

notes.h: Outcomes in the short and long term
notes.b: The march brought no immediate results. What helped Jarrow later came from other causes, chiefly rearmament.
points: In the short term there was no steelworks, no shipyard and no new commitment from the government, so unemployment in Jarrow stayed high.

Sir John Jarvis, Conservative MP for Guildford, organised help through a fund raised in Surrey. He brought shipbreaking (including the liner Olympic, broken up partly at Jarrow from 1935) and small metal works to the Palmers site, but they employed only a fraction of the jobless.
The Special Areas (Amendment) Act 1937 gave tax, rent and rate reliefs to firms in the special areas. There is no evidence that the march caused it.
Rearmament from the later 1930s and the Second World War brought work back to Tyneside, and this, not the march, ended mass unemployment in Jarrow.
Wilkinson published The Town That Was Murdered in 1939, and became Minister of Education in 1945 and died in 1947.
notes.tip: Marks reward the aims stated precisely (work, new industry, a steelworks), each failure with a fact (Baldwin's refusal, the petition ignored, the dole cut, no steelworks) and each partial success, then a clear judgement. Do not say the march caused the 1937 Act or rearmament orders.

notes.h: Significance, memory and the key concepts
notes.b: The march is remembered far more than it achieved. It became a symbol of the Depression and of how a democracy handled a peaceful protest.
points: The march became the best-known symbol of the hungry thirties and of government failure on unemployment.
Memories of the 1930s fed the post-1945 commitment to full employment and the welfare state.
The march was re-enacted in 1986, its 50th anniversary, and in 2011, its 75th anniversary, which shows its place in the memory of the labour movement.
The Depression: Jarrow was the extreme case of structural unemployment, meaning lasting joblessness caused by the decline of a whole industry, here shipbuilding, not a temporary dip.
Democracy: the march was a peaceful, lawful protest within a parliamentary democracy, in contrast to the extremism of the dictatorships and the violence of Cable Street in the same week.
It also showed the limits of democracy, since a petition could be ignored.
The NUWM's national marches were larger but are less remembered.
notes.tip: For comparison essays, say the march gave publicity but won nothing at the time. Keynes offered the policy answer that the government of 1936 did not use.

notes.b: The march took place in a month of major events, which helps date and judge any source about it.
points: The march set out the day after the Battle of Cable Street in London on 4 October 1936, when anti-fascists stopped a march by Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists.
The Spanish Civil War, which began in July 1936, was also in the news.
The NUWM's own national hunger march reached London in November 1936, and the Jarrow organisers had deliberately kept apart from it.
The abdication of Edward VIII in December 1936 pushed Jarrow from the headlines soon after the marchers had gone home.
Unemployment nationally was falling to under two million by late 1936, which strengthened the government's argument that special help was unnecessary.
notes.tip: A source's date helps place it. Ask whether it comes before or after the petition on 4 November, and whether it was written during the march or later.

notes.h: Placing a document: who said what and why
notes.b: Documents questions reward you for saying who wrote or issued a source, when and why, because that decides how far you can trust it.
points: Wilkinson's book of 1939 is a primary source by a participant, but it is partisan and was written after rearmament had begun to revive the town, so it combines a campaigner's anger with hindsight.
Government statements aimed to show that recovery was under way and to discourage marches on London, so they argue from recovery and constitutional practice.
Newspaper editorials written during the march are opinion, not a full account, so they show attitudes at the time more than they tell you what happened.
Photographs of the disciplined column with its banner support the image of respectability the organisers wanted.
Later textbooks are secondary sources, written by people who did not take part and who can use hindsight.
Labour and TUC leaders were cautious because they wished to avoid association with Communist-led marches and preferred action through Parliament.
notes.tip: Marks come from citing the document for each point. Say who issued the government's case, who wrote the 1939 book and when, and check who wrote a source before calling it primary.

notes.b: The judgement depends on whether the march is measured by its immediate aims or by its long-term effect on opinion.
points: Failure: the government refused to receive the marchers, no steelworks or shipyard was secured and the men lost benefit for the weeks they marched.
Failure: the real cause of recovery in Jarrow was rearmament and war, not the march.
Success: the march made Jarrow a national symbol, kept the problem of the distressed areas before the public and showed that the unemployed were disciplined and honest.
Success: it won wide sympathy across party lines in the town, and its memory shaped postwar attitudes to unemployment.
Contemporary view: supporters saw a moral victory, with dignity. Critics, among them Henson and Labour leaders, saw political theatre with no solution.
Later view: historians see it as a failure in its immediate aims but a lasting success in publicity and memory.
notes.tip: A good answer is usually a failure in its aims but not a total failure. Pair each failure with a fact and each success with a fact, then give one clear overall judgement.

keyTerms.definition: The worldwide economic slump that followed the Wall Street Crash of 1929, marked by falling output, bank failures and mass unemployment.
A system of government in which power rests with elected representatives or with the people, protected by free elections and the rule of law.
The depressed industrial regions of Britain, such as South Wales and the north-east, where unemployment remained high throughout the inter-war years.
The 1936 march of about 200 unemployed men from Jarrow to London to press the government for new industry for the town.
The company formed in 1930 to buy and close redundant shipyards, which bought the Palmers yard in 1934 and barred shipbuilding there for forty years.
The depressed regions of Britain designated in 1934 for government grants to attract new industries and public works.
The expansion of military forces and war industry in Britain from the mid-1930s, which brought new orders to Tyneside and reduced unemployment.
A formal written request signed by many people and presented to Parliament; Jarrow's carried over 11,000 signatures.
The national body set up under the Unemployment Act of 1934 to pay the long-term unemployed according to a household means test, which reduced the marchers' benefit.
A march of unemployed people to London to draw attention to unemployment, a tradition of the NUWM that Jarrow differed from by being cross-party.
